source_read: PMC HTML (PMC6890973; EClinicalMedicine 2019;16:81-97): abstract, Research in context, Introduction, Methods 2.1-2.8, Results 3.1-3.7 with Table 1 (all rows) and Table 2 (all rows and footnotes), Discussion 4-4.4, Conclusion, acknowledgements, disclosures, funding. Forest plots (Figs 2-3) and PRISMA figure are images; values taken from text and tables. Supplements A-G (.docx) not opened.

claims.overstatement: Slight. 'After adjustment for demographics, other substance use and premorbid risk' paraphrases Table 2's D/O/P flags, which say the effect persisted after adjustment for these factors; whether each of the 4 pooled studies adjusted for all three is not shown in the main text (Supplement E). 'Than people who do not' should note that most comparisons were made within substance-using samples, so the comparator often used other drugs (Results 3.1, last paragraph). No causal wording, which matches the evidence levels (B/C for unadjusted, E for the adjusted pool).
claims.note: All numbers reproduce from Table 2 and Results 3.3. The any-use n of 3436 counts 1064 person-month observations from 278 people in McKetin 2013 (Table 2 footnote b); Table 1's study Ns sum to 3469. The single adjusted any-use estimate is the within-person OR 5.3 (3.4-8.3) from McKetin 2013. For any use, symptoms OR 2.7 (1.5-4.7) vs disorders 1.3 (1.0-1.9, p=0.087). Frequency of use could not be meta-analysed because measures were too heterogeneous (Methods 2.7; Limitations 4.2).

anchors.extracted: Any use vs no use: OR 2.0 (1.3-3.3), 7 studies, n 3436, I2 80%, evidence level C, quality 77%. Use disorder vs none: OR 3.0 (1.9-4.8), 13 studies, n 81,316, I2 90%, level B, quality 75%; adjusted OR 2.4 (1.6-3.5), 4 studies, n 7648, I2 35%, level E (cross-sectional among drug users), quality 88%, flagged D/O/P.

Symptoms vs diagnosed disorder. Any use: symptoms OR 2.7 (1.5-4.7), I2 80%; disorder OR 1.3 (1.0-1.9), p=0.087, I2 0%. Use disorder: symptoms OR 4.3 (2.9-6.5), I2 47%; disorder OR 2.3 (1.2-4.7), I2 93%.

anchors.locator: Table 2 footnote b; Table 1 footnote a; Results 3.1, last paragraph
anchors.extracted: The only adjusted any-use estimate (OR 5.3, 3.4-8.3) is McKetin 2013's within-person estimate from 1064 months of observation in 278 people; most comparisons were within substance-using samples; 17 adjusted any-use and 9 adjusted use-disorder comparisons in all.
Frequency-of-use and route comparisons not meta-analysed because measures were too heterogeneous; authors state it remains unclear what level of use conveys a risk.

Authors judge psychosis the most compelling case for causation, but say evidence for schizophrenia is more tenuous and that premorbid factors (familial risk, trauma, perinatal factors, migration, urbanicity) were not controlled; unadjusted estimates likely inflated by confounding.

claims.overstatement: Mild generalization. In the any-use pool, all but one study measured depressive symptoms rather than diagnosed depression (Results 3.6, 1st paragraph), and for amphetamine use disorder versus none there was no significant association with major depression (OR 1.2, 0.5-2.7; 6 studies; I2 87%), which the claim does not mention. The general-population (2.0) and substance-using-sample (1.1) figures are unadjusted subgroup estimates; the claim does not say so.
claims.note: The 1.60 and 1.50 cohort estimates come from Leung et al. (2023), not this source. This source adds two longitudinal studies supporting direction (Briere 2012: adolescent use preceded later depressive symptoms after adjustment; Glasner-Edwards 2009: depression fell in treatment entrants who stopped using). Authors suggest the small adjusted association may be largely generic to substance use and shared risk factors (Discussion, 5th paragraph).

anchors.extracted: Any use: unadjusted OR 1.6 (1.1-2.2), 7 studies, n 19,526, I2 80%; adjusted OR 1.3 (1.2-1.4), 6 studies, n 2684, I2 0%, quality 87%, level C, flagged D/O/P. All but one study assessed depressive symptoms. Longitudinal support: Briere 2012; Glasner-Edwards 2009.

General-population samples: OR 2.0 (1.6-2.4), I2 11% (5 studies); substance-using samples: OR 1.1 (0.7-1.7), I2 76%. Use disorder vs none (major depression outcomes): OR 1.2 (0.5-2.7), 6 studies, I2 87%; one adjusted twin study 2.8 (0.6-11.8); null attributed to samples with heavy substance use or other clinical conditions.

claims.overstatement: None. The claim uses Table 2's any-use adjusted OR 1.7 (1.0-2.9); the Results text (3.5) gives 1.4 for the same estimate, an internal inconsistency in the source.
claims.note: The use-disorder adjusted pool (Toles 2006, Kalechstein 2000, Matsumoto 2012, McCullumsmith 2013) mixes suicidal ideation, 'severe suicidality' and attempts, all cross-sectional among drug users (level E, quality 62%). The 3.6 for attempts is an unadjusted any-use estimate. No longitudinal evidence on whether use preceded suicidality (Discussion).

anchors.extracted: Use disorder: unadjusted OR 2.3 (1.8-2.9), 7 studies, n 23,302, I2 57%; adjusted OR 1.5 (1.3-1.8), 4 studies, n 21,753, I2 0%, level E, quality 62%. Any use: unadjusted OR 4.4 (2.4-8.2), 7 studies, I2 84%; adjusted OR 1.7 (1.0-2.9), 4 studies, n 7066, I2 77%, quality 74%.
Text gives the adjusted ORs as 1.4 (any use) and 1.5 (use disorder), 'substantially smaller' than unadjusted; Table 2 and abstract give 1.7 for any use.

Suicide attempts with any use: OR 3.6 (2.2-5.9), I2 46%, 6 studies; suicidal ideation with use disorder: OR 2.2 (1.8-2.8), I2 22%, 5 studies. Only one study examined completed suicide (Tunving 1988, treatment entrants): suicides higher than expected but not significantly above opioid users; most cases had premorbid risk.
Quality of suicidality evidence poor; no longitudinal evidence on sequence; association small after adjustment; weaker outcome measures for suicidality and violence (Results 3.1).

claims.overstatement: Minor wording. 'Self-reported violent behaviour' versus 'violent offending' implies a self-report versus records contrast that the source does not make: the violent-behaviour pool (refs 47-51) includes interviewer-rated BPRS hostility (McKetin 2014), violent behaviour recorded in an emergency department (Bunting 2007), self-reported violence (Iritani 2007), sexual exploitation/abuse (Sigurdsson 2010) and BSI hostility (Nyamathi 2014); the violent-offending pool (refs 45, 52-55) includes self-reported violent acts (Cartier 2006), Opiate Treatment Index self-report (Barrett 2013), confessions (Miura 2006) and charges (Greene 1973). Better: 'violent behaviour and hostility measures were associated (OR 3.7) but violent offending was not (OR 1.0)'. 'Lowest quality ratings': violence pools scored 56% (unadjusted, tied with unadjusted any-use suicidality), 58% (adjusted, lowest adjusted pool) and 43% (single use-disorder study), so 'lowest or tied lowest' is exact.
claims.note: 'Not established' matches the non-significant adjusted pool (1.4, 0.8-2.4), but the interval also includes moderate associations, and the authors note significant large effects in two population surveys and two longitudinal studies (one within-person, adjusted for concurrent substance use), concluding there 'may be' an association needing confirmation.

anchors.extracted: Any use: unadjusted OR 2.2 (1.2-4.1), 10 studies, n 30,084, I2 95%, quality 56%; adjusted OR 1.4 (0.8-2.4), 6 studies, n 26,289, I2 25%, quality 58%, not significant. Use disorder: one study, OR 6.2 (3.1-12.3), quality 43%.

Violent behaviour: OR 3.7 (3.1-4.5), I2 34% (refs 47-51); violent offending: OR 1.0 (0.4-2.7), I2 94% (refs 45, 52-55). Longitudinal: more violent behaviour during periods of use after adjustment for concurrent substance use (McKetin 2014); higher violent recidivism after release with use disorder (Watanabe 2005). Authors: poor study quality limits causal inference; there 'may be' an association.

key_findings.correction: Subgroup ORs confirmed. 'Lowest of any outcome (56 to 58%)' should be 'lowest or tied lowest': unadjusted suicidality pools scored 56% (any use) and 57% (use disorder) against violence's 56% (unadjusted) and 58% (adjusted); the single use-disorder violence study scored 43%. The card's own validity_norms field states this correctly.

reporting_issues.note: Reference list checked: [29]=[105] McKetin 2013; [47]=[106] McKetin 2014; [57]=[107] Sutherland 2015; [61]=[108] Capra 2015.
[109] is Walls, Freedenthal and Wisneski 2008 (Soc Work), not in Table 1.

risk_of_bias.note: Critically low under AMSTAR 2 rules (publication bias not assessed; no excluded-study list in the article). Caveat shared with the card: the list of excluded studies might be in the unread supplements.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor; the Discussion grades evidence by outcome and is restrained.

missed: Table 1 gives Callaghan 2012 an N of 10,815,900 (36,162 exposed), yet Table 2's total n for the 13-study use-disorder psychosis pool that includes it is 81,316 (the other 12 studies sum to about 13,243 in Table 1); the comparison actually analysed for that study is not explained.

In the violent-offending subgroup (Results 3.4, refs 45, 52-55), reference [55] is Sutherland et al. 2018, a typology of new psychoactive substance use in the general Australian population, which does not match a violent-offending study; [57] (Sutherland 2015, violent offence perpetration) appears intended. Same pattern as the card's reporting issues 1-2.

For cl_meth_depression: the claim omits that the any-use association was with depressive symptoms in all but one study and that amphetamine use disorder showed no significant association with major depression (OR 1.2, 0.5-2.7); the card records the null in key findings 3 and 8, but the claim should carry it.
Minor: any-use psychosis n is 3436 in Table 2 against 3469 summed from Table 1 (including 1064 person-months from 278 people); Results 3.6 calls 5 of 7 depression studies 'half'.
